depth: The depth map captures the downward-sloping ground plane of the paved road and left-side dirt shoulder stretching from roughly 3 to 5 m below the camera wearer to within about 0.5–1.5 m ahead, with no other people present in the scene. In frames 1 and 2, the camera wearer's own legs (around 3–5 m away at the bottom center-right) and outstretched hands (far and out of reach at 3–5 m at the bottom right and left) appear brighter than the road surface, while a partial vehicle wheel on the upper right of frame 2 (about 1.8 m away) and a round leaf bowl to its left (about 2.2 m away and 3–5 m from the wheel) stand out against the darker background. Across frames 2 to 4, the camera wearer moves away from and bends toward the bowl as it shifts from the upper center to the lower-right foreground and brightens markedly while remaining far and out of reach (about 3–5 m away) while being held by the wearer's hand at the bottom edge, before the view tilts up in frame 5 to show the receding road within about 0.5–1.5 m ahead. The map clearly separates the 3D relief of the raised tire, the concave bowl rim, and the wearer's limbs from the flat asphalt—which is harder to gauge in RGB alone—and shows the limbs, tire, and held bowl partly clipped by the lower and right frame boundaries. However, the monocular depth scale is inconsistent across frames, rendering the bowl in frame 3 as a floating mid-grey disc darker than the surrounding ground at the same distance and over-brightening the left-hand road edge in frame 5 as if it were an obstacle 3–5 m away.
segmentation: The instance segmentation map leaves the paved road, dirt shoulder, and frame 2 vehicle wheel unlabelled in black, isolating only fragments of the camera wearer's body at the bottom of frames 1–2 and the leaf bowl in frame 3–4, while confirming no other people are present or facing away from the camera wearer. In frames 1 and 2, the wearer's right hand, lower legs/feet (3–5 m below), and left hand (far and out of reach at 3–5 m on the bottom left) are split into separatecoloured masks labelled 'person' that are partially cut off by the bottom frame edge and separated by about 3–5 m laterally. As the camera wearer walks forward and reaches down in frame 4, the leaf bowl—now held far out of reach at 3–5 m in the lower-right foreground—is segmented as a large tan mask, whereas in frames 2, 3, and 5 the bowl on the ground (3–5 m ahead) and the wearer's fingertips at the bottom edge are completely missed. This map provides crisp pixel boundaries between the wearer's limbs and the ground in frames 1–2 and outlines the held bowl in frame 4 where the wearer's fingers slightly occlude its bottom rim. However, it is highly unreliable in both semantics and recall: it splits a single ego-body into multiple 'person' instances, misclassifies the distant leaf bowl as a 'sandwich', hallucinates a purple 'surfboard' mask on a patch of dirt/concrete at the top-left edge of frame 3 (about 2 m away), and fails to detect any objects in frame 5.
pose: The pose map renders only magenta hand skeletons against a black background with no yellow body skeletons, reflecting that no other people are in the scene and that the camera wearer's head and torso are behind the egocentric viewpoint facing forward and downward along the road. In frames 1 and 2, a single magenta hand skeleton tracks the camera wearer's left hand in the lower-left foreground, far and out of reach (roughly 3–5 m in front of and below the camera, about 3–5 m to the left of the wearer's legs), with the palm angled inward and fingers curled slightly toward the ground. Across frames 1 to 2, this left hand shifts slightly downward and to the left as the wearer steps forward away from the tire (1.8 m away on the right) and the leaf bowl (2.2 m away on the left), before disappearing below the frame in frame 3 as the wearer moves away from the bowl. The map makes the fine 3D finger articulation and joint orientation of the wearer's left hand much clearer than the motion-blurred RGB frames alone. However, it is unreliable for full-scene body tracking because it misses the wearer's partially visible right hand at the bottom-right of frame 1, fails to detect the visible legs and feet in frames 1–3, and misses the left hand gripping the lower rim of the bowl at the bottom edge of frame 4.
